page.title: Best Cheap 85mm Lens for Sony (2026): Meike SE Mark II vs Viltrox EVO vs Sony
page.desc: The cheapest autofocus 85mm for Sony full frame is the Meike 85mm F1.8 SE Mark II at $199.99. Here is how it compares with the Viltrox 85mm f/2 EVO, Viltrox 85mm f/1.8 II, 7Artisans and Sony's own FE 85mm f/1.8.
page.intro:
Short answer. The best cheap 85mm lens for Sony is the Meike 85mm F1.8 SE Mark II ({buy:meike-85mm-f1-8-se-mark-ii-sony-e}): $199.99, f/1.8, focuses to 0.65 m (2.1 ft) and weighs 369 g (13 oz). It is the lowest-priced full-frame 85mm with autofocus for E mount from any maker, and in Fstoppers' test single-shot autofocus was quiet and accurate on a Sony a7CR, with continuous AF locking on faster than expected at the price. If you can spend $75 more, the Viltrox AF 85mm f/2 EVO ($275 on viltrox.com, 2026-11-06) is the better all-round lens: a third of a stop slower, but with a clicked aperture ring, 360 g, and autofocus that LensTip found accurate on every body it tried. For moving kids, events or rain, Sony's own FE 85mm f/1.8 (about $650) still wins on tracking, a focus-hold button and dust and moisture resistance.

Both budget lenses share the same weak spots: softness and color fringing wide open at close range, visible focus breathing in video, and only a mount gasket for weather protection. The Meike's 11 aperture blades give rounder highlights than the Viltrox's nine. On an APS-C body such as an a6400 or a6700, either lens becomes a 127 mm equivalent, which is long for indoor portraits.

page.after:
What owners and reviewers complain about

Across the reviews we read, the same four issues came up for every budget 85, so they are not reasons to pick one brand over another. Close-focus softness and color fringing at the widest aperture was noted for the Meike SE Mark II three times and for the Viltrox EVO twice; it clears by f/4. Focus breathing in video came up for the Meike twice, for the Viltrox EVO twice and for the Viltrox 85mm f/1.8 II once. Minimal weather sealing (a mount gasket, or none on the Viltrox f/1.8 II) came up four times. Autofocus speed is the one that splits them: the Meike's single-shot AF was called accurate on a Sony a7CR, but a lab test on Nikon Z measured small direction-dependent focus errors, while Cameralabs measured the heavier Viltrox 85mm f/1.8 II at 93.6% repeatability with occasional hunting. One Adorama buyer of the earlier Meike noted a short lag after pressing the shutter. Nobody we found reported the lens failing to talk to the camera; all three budget lenses have full electronic contacts and USB-C firmware updates.

Which cheap 85mm by need

Lowest price, stills first: the Meike 85mm F1.8 SE Mark II at $199.99. You get f/1.8, the closest focus of the group at 0.65 m, and 11 blades. Shoot at f/2.8 for close head shots and the fringing goes away.

Best lens under $300: the Viltrox AF 85mm f/2 EVO at $275. It is 9 g lighter, takes cheaper 58 mm filters, focuses accurately on every body LensTip tried, and the clicked aperture ring doubles as a smooth video ring. You give up a third of a stop and 9 cm of close focus.

Video with focus pulls: the Meike 85mm f1.8 Pro ({buy:meike-85mm-f1-8-pro-sony-e}). Fstoppers found no focus breathing and smooth tracking, and it has a metal aperture ring. It costs $140 more than the SE Mark II and is sharper stopped down than wide open.

Moving subjects, weddings, rain: Sony FE 85mm f/1.8. Native linear-motor AF tracks faster, it has a focus-hold button and a dust and moisture resistant barrel. At about $650 it costs more than three Meikes, and used copies sell for far less.

Not recommended

Viltrox AF 85mm f/1.8 II at $329: Cameralabs measured one of the poorest focus repeatability results it has tested, found no gasket at the mount, and it weighs 548 g. Viltrox's own 85mm f/2 EVO is cheaper and better in every test we read.

7Artisans AF 85mm F1.8 at $299: priced above both the Meike and the Viltrox EVO, launch coverage called autofocus its weak point, and we found no independent test showing it beating either.

Any manual-focus 85mm for portraits: the Meike, 7Artisans and TTArtisan manual 85s are cheaper, but at f/1.8 the depth of field on an eye is a few millimeters, and reviewers of the autofocus Meike report Eye AF working on Sony bodies. Save manual glass for video.
